title: Show HN: Spotatui, a Spotify TUI/GUI without web API rate limits
text:
About 11 months ago i revived the amazing but unfortunately unmaintained spotify-tui. Since then I have been working on it almost non stop, finding a lot of problems on the way.

One of the main issues I ran into were the Spotify web API rate limits. Third party clients like spotatui are dependent on a developer app made in the Spotify developer dashboard, which get rate limited a lot and Spotify has slowly been deprecating endpoints from it. The workaround for this used to be using a shared client id from ncspot but unfortunately that got rate limited too. This is when i started adding other playback sources, including YouTube, Navidrome/Subsonic, Internet radio with +- 30.000 stations, local files, Qobuz for lossless audio and Apple Music for macOS only where it controls the music app remotely.

I fixed both the deprecated endpoints and the rate limits with one solution. It still uses librespot in the back, my spotatui specific fork, but gets all data from it instead of only playback. The data comes from the internal API of the official clients, that API gives metadata, playlists, the user library, devices, lyrics and audio analysis. For searching it uses Pathfinder, the internal GraphQL API.

There are no web API rate limits because there is no shared app quota. Every user uses their own session as if it was the official client. The only potential problem is that Spotify does not document this API so any change on their side would break it. I intend to fix any of those issues as soon as they pop up.

It all started as a TUI back in 2019 but since then I've added a GUI to it too. The GUI is still a bit behind the TUI in terms of features, it only ships Spotify for now, but full parity between the TUI and GUI is coming soon. After that full parity with the official client is next. That is also why I made the GUI looks almost the same as the official client. That way its easier for me and users to find missing features.

Spotatui also has lua scripting support, a optional Web companion on spotatui.com, and if you have a AI coding agent like ChatGPT codex or Claude Code you can enable the MCP tools, which lets AI become your personal DJ just by talking to it.

Its written in Rust, uses ratatui for the terminal UI and Tauri 2 for the GUI. The Rust core starts a small web server with localhost that only your pc can reach which the GUI then serves. Both frontends share the same playback logic, the same login and the same Spotify code. The only difference is how you interact with it.

On first launch it opens a web browser where you need to login with your Spotify premium account (premium is not optional), that is the whole setup done. I would love any feedback about bugs you encounter or features you would like to see. GitHub: https://github.com/LargeModGames/spotatui Releases: https://github.com/LargeModGames/spotatui/releases/latest Website: https://spotatui.com/

Thanks to librespot for making this all possible

- DAG Structures: defining a structured task node <> edge relationship graph can be leveraged directly - great performance boost, particularly for CLI agents, since Claude Opus 4.5

There was a good discussion about that here recently. I think people are misinterpreting the bitter lesson a bit.

It tells you that you don't need to craft special strategies for pinning, holding the centre and so on to make a program that's good at chess; you just need general-purpose search, general-purpose optimization and tons of training data.

It does not say that a fully general LLM or similar will necessarily be better at chess than a neural net trained against the chess rules and nothing else. There's no reason to think that any of the non-chess knowledge encoded in the LLM will be of any use in playing chess. To the contrary, the bitter lesson says that absolutely nothing besides the chess rules is needed. That's exactly why human-crafted strategies turn out not to be helpful.

An LLM on its own will never ever beat Stockfish, pound for pound. (Of course it doesn't need to, it can just use Stockfish.)

So I'd say problem-specific models will always beat general models, as long as the problem domain and scoring are completely defined, like chess and go are. It's CPUs versus ASICs. As soon as the problem is open-ended, a general model probably wins. Driving is in that category, although maybe on the borderline -- driving in very specific environments is close to fully defined. laya-guard is a local check that occurs before any coding agent tool call, deciding whether to approve, send for review, or block the call.

Regex policies catch known dangerous patterns before even reaching models, any command that is blocked is never seen by models, commands like ls, git status, and npm test will skip the model altogether, unless they have pipes, chaining, redirects, -exec flags, or sensitive paths, everything else is sent to the model for processing, once you have the model downloaded, it makes decisions from a fixed set of outcomes with no API key or request needed for any external service, there are also hooks for 11 different agents including Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and many more.

And Also a local dashboard where you can see all decision and why it was made and install the hook for each agent, it doesn't save the commands themeslves.

In my tests with AgentDojo, it blocked 25/27 attacks, and allowed 92/97 harmless tasks, it correctly identified 64/66 commands I made.

After the Reddit post, people have found some issues with it:

Adding a comment at the end of a command would fool the model to not block the command.

The model only read the first 4,000 characters, so it could be spammed with junk to the beginning to bypass the check, this would send dangerous commands like curl to review.

"curl" repeated 40,000 times caused one regex to run for 48 seconds, timing out the hook and running the command.

All 3 issues have already been fixed, somebody also pointed out that if the server was down, commands ran without any check, now it asks you first, or blocks the command if the agent can't ask

Please note that this is not a tool to check if the code written is correct, it's a tool to prevent agents from running dangerous commands.

Edison industrialized the creation of patents (e.g. he would hire thousands of bright young graduates, and have them invent things, and then patent them in his own name). I once read a book that said Thomas Edison was the "greatest inventor" because he held thousands of patents. The reality is that he invented a tiny fraction of those patents, and he merely put his name on the work of other people.

My point is, if the auto-software-patent scenario becomes true, then wealthy people/organizations/oligopolies will create a patent-factory, made of either people, LLMs, or (more likely) both.

Heyo!

I'm Adit, an undergrad in Finland. This is a preview of a side project I worked on last weekend. Essentially, Dragonfly is a LoRA fine-tune of Qwen3-VL with typed output heads that answers many questions about an image in one pass, with a probability for every answer. Unlike a VLM that generates an answer to each question, Dragonfly reads the image once and scores every question in the same pass. Questions can't see each other, so each answer is the same as asking it alone, in any order.

Instead of text outputs, Dragonfly answers with calibrated probabilities for the options you give it in order to answer the question. You can ask Dragonfly multiple choice, yes/no, or scale-based questions.

As you might have guessed already, I got the idea from Jev and thought it would be fun to train a small model that can do the same thing for images. There wasn't a dataset for questions specifically, so I compiled a couple open datasets to form around half of our training data and then distilled Qwen to generate ~300k questions that I could verify against the human annotated data.

Over the last few weeks I've really been using Codex and Claude to solve a lot of parallel tasks, across a lot of different projects. This lead me to wishing that I could interface with my agents in the same way that I interface with my already existing windows and editors. I think it depends on your definition for 'intelligence'. IIRC, Wikipedia lists 15 different definitions for 'intelligence'. One common ground is 'the ability to solve problems', which covers some aspects of how the term 'intelligence' is usually used, but not necessarily everything.

If your 'problem' as a cell is to feed yourself, it is a clever apparatus that solves that problem, and can be depicted as intelligent.

If you understand the 'fully automatic mechanism' completely, you agree that it solves a problem, but you deny that this is intelligent. However, the denial depends on your understanding of the mechanism. If you assume that the world is deterministic (that means, every effect has a definite cause, to put it simply), we cannot be something other than a 'fully automatic mechanism', however a very, very complicated one that we do not fully understand. Indeed, in a deterministic world nothing can be different from a 'fully automatic mechanism', and, by your implied definition of intelligence, nothing can be intelligent. This conclusion leaves the definition of intelligence as something 'other than fully automatic mechanism' rather useless, as it does not distinguish anything. (If you do assume that the world is not deterministic, a similar argument still holds, as long as you do not imply that a person can determine the outcome of the non-determinism, which sounds strange to me to imply.)

I think what you want for something to call 'intelligent', is that you don't immediately understand how the mechanism works and the assumption of some kind of thought process and/or planning. The first property unfortunately depends on what you might consider your own intelligence, which makes it difficult as an objective measure of intelligence so that you can argue about it in a forum. The second property (thinking/planning) might be present in the cell in a way that you don't see (eg. see storage of the current value of 'now') and, similary, it might not be present in us humans in the way self-perceive it.

More than once did I experience a seemingly 'intelligent system' that I found fasciniating, which, after I studied it, I did not think of as intelligent anymore (eg. my first impressions of Weizenbaum's Eliza), which for the aforementioned reasons I think is kind-of silly of me.

text:
shadowclone reads the coding-agent sessions already on your disk, finds where you corrected the agent and turns those corrections into skills your agents load next time. It supports Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Pi, and Antigravity. Every capture source is off by default and has its own consent setting.

Why I'm building it?

I use multiple harnesses and agents, I extensively use Claud Code and Codex, but I also use Cursor and Antigravity every now and then. I didn't want to have to teach every harness or model the things I taught the other ones between my last session and the current one. I also cannot have my personal rules and preferences in all the repositories I work on because my collaborators may have varying levels of trust with AI and their own preferences. shadowclone helps me build and improve trust with my agents so I can give them more autonomy while running multiple sessions in parallel.

---

Who is this for?

If you only use Claude or Codex or any one of these, you may not need the shadowclone CLI and the harness and agent you use might already be sufficient. But, if you are like me and work across harnesses and agents, shadowclone will help you avoid repeating your preferences each time.

---

Built-in skills and skill builds

shadowclone is also great for someone who is just now adopting AI into their coding workflows because it ships with several skills that they can use to customize their agent's behavior. They can equip all the skills, or just some of them, they'll see the "personality" their agent gets from equipping those skills from the `shadowclone wizard`.

---

Setup is extremely easy, just ask your Claude Code, or Codex, or another agent -

"Set up shadowclone: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/theonly1me/shadowclone/mai..."

---

Privacy

shadowclone is free and open source, it uses the MIT license. It doesn't have a subscription, or a server. It just uses your existing agent subscription i.e. Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Antigravity, or even your local model via Pi. You can explicitly disable sources, it also redacts any and all sensitive information it uses for learning.

---

PR reviews and Cloud bots

It can review PRs with the `shadowclone review` command, it ships a guided review skill that will perform a deep review of your code (or someone else's) and produce an HTML document you can annotate, add comments to and submit so your agent can stage a draft review on the PR you are reviewing.

---

Evals

I performed several evals, I won't describe them here, all of them are available in the repository - https://github.com/theonly1me/shadowclone/tree/main/evals

---

Comparison to other tools?

You can also see how it compares to other tools here - https://github.com/theonly1me/shadowclone/tree/main#how-shad...

The things that actually cost me time were not CPU or RAM, though. First, network policy. I run untrusted code with an egress allowlist, and most launched projects assume open internet, so the useful knob is per-sandbox allowlist editing with a proxy for package registries, not more memory. Second, environment hygiene. The sandbox needs a clean env with no inherited secrets, and a persistent sandbox that does not pick up changed env vars or allowlist entries without a restart bit me more than once. Third, a wall-clock timebox per run, because a stuck npm install behind a proxy fails silently rather than loudly.
